name: AI Observatory
blurb: Live telemetry on the health of the field: release cadence, repository activity, uptime, GPU availability, funding, patents, and regulatory movement.

built.name: Model Release Cadence
built.detail: How fast new models are shipping, and by whom.

built.name: Repository Activity
built.detail: This section tracks GitHub star counts and push activity across 55 widely used open-source AI repositories, spanning frameworks like TensorFlow and PyTorch, inference tools like Ollama and llama.cpp, and newer agent projects like AutoGPT and browser-use.

built.name: Hugging Face Trends
built.detail: This section tracks Hugging Face model activity: total download volume across roughly 16,363 tracked models, the most-downloaded individual models, and the license types those models are published under.

built.name: API Uptime
built.detail: This section tracks measured uptime for 12 AI API providers, including Anthropic, OpenAI, Cohere, Groq, Cerebras, Deepgram, ElevenLabs, AssemblyAI, Stability AI, Baseten, Fireworks AI, and Lambda.

built.name: Cloud GPU and Compute Telemetry
built.detail: What can be lawfully measured about AI compute: quarterly capital expenditure from the seven companies whose capex is the buildout, read from their own XBRL facts on SEC EDGAR, plus GPU cloud service health and verified benchmark registries.

built.name: Funding Activity
built.detail: This section is meant to track capital flowing into AI companies by funding stage and sector.

built.name: Patent Filings
built.detail: This section tracks cumulative AI-related patent counts for 108 companies, ranking them by total portfolio size and charting how the combined total moves over time.

built.name: Security Incidents
built.detail: This section tracks open incidents reported on the status pages of 12 AI infrastructure and model providers, including Anthropic, OpenAI, Cohere, Lambda, Fireworks AI, Baseten, Deepgram, and ElevenLabs.

title: AI Observatory
answer: Live telemetry on the health of the field: release cadence, repository activity, uptime, GPU availability, funding, patents, and regulatory movement.

reading.body:
The observatory's most concrete measurements are of software and services, not of compute: 55 repositories, roughly 16,363 Hugging Face models, 12 API providers, and 108 companies' patent portfolios.

The pattern across the sections is that the field is instrumented where data is public and cheap to collect. GitHub stars and pushes, Hugging Face downloads and licenses, status-page uptime, and patent counts are all readable from open endpoints. The compute section is the exception and is explicitly framed as "what can be lawfully measured": quarterly capital expenditure from seven companies, taken from their own XBRL facts on SEC EDGAR, plus GPU cloud service health and benchmark registries. That phrasing is the honest part. Capital expenditure is a financial disclosure, not a measurement of delivered power or silicon, and the section does not claim otherwise.

For AI specifically, the split matters because the binding constraints sit on the compute side, and that is the side with the thinnest direct telemetry. Release cadence, repository activity, and download volume tell you how fast software is moving. They do not tell you whether the grid, the buildings, or the chips can keep up. The seven-company capex series is a proxy for intent to build, reported quarterly and lagging. GPU cloud service health tells you whether rented capacity is reachable, not how much of it exists.

What the data does not cover is as clear as what it does. Funding Activity is described as something the section "is meant to track," which is not the same as tracking it. Regulatory movement appears in the summary but has no corresponding section. There are no grid, power, or datacenter figures anywhere in the structure, so any claim about electricity as the constraint cannot be sourced from this page. The counts are also uneven in kind: 16,357 appears both as a model count and as the count attached to release cadence, and the provider lists overlap heavily between uptime and incidents, so the 12 and 13 figures describe nearly the same set of companies rather than independent populations.
